source.title: The Devil behind the mask: An emergent safety vulnerability of Diffusion LLMs
source.authors: Zichen Wen; Jiashu Qu; Zhao-Run Chen; Xiao-Ya Lu; Dong-Rui Liu; Zhiyuan Liu; Rui Wu; Yicun Yang; Xiangqi Jin; Haoyun Xu; Xu-Yang Liu; Wei-Jia Li; Chao-Chao Lu; Jing Shao; Cong-Hui He; Lin-Feng Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether changing response-generation length changes refusal versus harmful output on a diffusion LLM. This is a different method and architecture from the original claims.
record.gate_note: The study does not test fine-tuning on small harmful or benign datasets, token-position KL, localized safety weights, or why safety is shallow. Its interleaved mask-text jailbreak is a distinct attack rather than a compliant-opening prefill or suffix. Main attack success results are recorded as findings about a related, uncovered mask-infill vulnerability. The targeted refusal fine-tuning in Appendix A is evaluated against that attack, but does not test whether safety is distributed beyond initial response tokens.
record.test_reason: DIJA fixes compliant scaffold text on the assistant side of the response and lets the model fill masked spans. The authors (App. B.7) describe this as a generalization of prefilling attacks, with user control over assistant output. DIJA defeats refusal in safety-tuned diffusion LLMs, a new architecture, which bears on V4. Appendix A trains refusals that the authors frame as adapting deep alignment (V7), evaluated against the same attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that bidirectional modeling and parallel decoding make dLLMs vulnerable to interleaved mask-text prompts, despite safety comparable to autoregressive models under standard attacks. They explicitly relate DIJA to prefilling attacks. They frame their refusal-aware denoising alignment as adapting deep alignment (Qi et al. 2024) to dLLMs, reporting reduced but nonzero attack success at modest capability cost.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a masked-span jailbreak and response-length variation, not the original fine-tuning-data or per-token KL methods. It also presents targeted refusal-aware denoising alignment.
record.method_sensitivity: Generation length changes the illustrated LLaDA-1.5 response: length 256 refuses while length 512 produces potentially harmful content. DIJA attack performance also varies across victim models and benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: The prompt-level defenses Self-reminder and RPO produce no significant reduction in DIJA success on three dLLMs (Fig 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prompt-based jailbreak defenses designed for autoregressive models fail against assistant-side mask-infill attacks on dLLMs.

record.problems: The generation-length result is an illustrative single query rather than a rate over a prompt set. The main attack tables report no uncertainty for their comparisons. The authors report standard deviations for repeated runs and human validation of the GPT-4o harmfulness judge.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: ASR-k and harmfulness-score metrics alongside the ASR-e rows, the code-oriented model tables (Tables 6–8), attack baselines, defense conditions, and targeted-alignment results (Table 4). These are further results for the separate mask-infill attack or its defense rather than tests of the named claim versions; the targeted alignment specifically trains refusal for those prompts. The appendix also reports prompt diversity, attack stability, and mask-span ablations (Tables 9–12), which do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
Autoregressive models, adversarial suffixes as an attack, and prefix-only prefilling on dLLMs are not tested.
The causes proposed (bidirectional modeling, parallel decoding) are hypothesized, not tested. Data and objective causes are not examined.
Not tested: whether the aligned model's safety spreads beyond early positions, and whether it holds against unseen attacks, prefills or fine-tuning. The authors list generalization as future work.

missing.what: Ablation: without masking, ASR-e is 14.0%; without separators, 16.8%; full DIJA, 55.5% (LLaDA-Instruct, HarmBench). This is the key control for scaffold prefilling.
Number of mask spans, fixed 50-token budget: ASR-e 31.5% (1 span), 55.5% (3 spans), 43.5% (10 spans).
Effect of masked-token count on ASR-e, HS and SRS across four dLLMs; success is limited at 10 tokens and declines at 50.
DIJA results on code dLLMs (DiffuCoder Instruct and cpGRPO, Dream-Coder), e.g. JailbreakBench ASR-e rises 12→76.
StrongREJECT SRS for DIJA versus zero-shot across four dLLMs.
Refusal-aware alignment: DIJA ASR-e before and after alignment, plus general capability benchmarks.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the DIJA rows to none. Because the threat model assumes assistant-side editing and the authors position DIJA as generalized prefilling, these rows bear on V4 in a new architecture. Hence T3 rather than T2. The V7 link is loose: the training pairs attack prompts with refusals, not recovery after harmful prefixes. The rows record no uncertainty, but Table 10 shows run-to-run SD below 0.7%.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples make a safety-trained model comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
No aligned/base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
The study varies generation length, but does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or other decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization, ablation, or safety-weight edit.
The paper proposes architectural explanations for its mask-infill vulnerability but does not test whether data or training objectives cause first-token shallowness.
The targeted refusal-aware training is not evaluated for whether safety is spread beyond early response tokens or holds up across broader attack patterns.

relationships.reason: ASR-e rises from near-zero or low zero-shot rates to 55–90% (r3, r4, r5, r7, r8, r9, r10). Removing the masks drops ASR-e to 14.0% (Table 11, not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: ASR-e rose from near-zero or low zero-shot rates to 55–90%, and removing the masks dropped it to 14.0%.

relationships.condition: MMaDA-MixCoT on HarmBench, and scaffold structure choices
relationships.reason: The gain is smaller for MMaDA on HarmBench (29.0% to 46.8%, r6). Per the text, success depends on interleaving: a single span gives ASR-e 31.5% versus 55.5% (Table 12), and 10 masked tokens give limited success (Fig 7).
relationships.display_finding: The gain on MMaDA-MixCoT for HarmBench was smaller, from 29.0% to 46.8%. Success depended on interleaving: a single span gave 31.5% versus 55.5%, and 10 masked tokens gave only limited success.

source_check.condition: MMaDA-MixCoT on HarmBench, and scaffold structure choices
source_check.reason: MMaDA-MixCoT rises from 29.0% to 46.8% ASR-e (r6), a smaller gain than the other models. Table 12 reports 31.5% for one span versus 55.5% for three spans at a fixed 50-token mask budget; Section 5 reports limited effectiveness with 10 masks per segment.

relationships.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct after refusal-aware denoising alignment on 10k DIJA-style prompts, evaluated on DIJA
relationships.reason: Based on text (Table 4, no row). ASR-e falls 55.5→32.5 on HarmBench and 81→25 on JailbreakBench but is not eliminated. GPQA drops 32.4→27.5 and BBH 51.5→47.8 (Table 5). Only the in-distribution attack was tested.
relationships.display_finding: ASR-e fell from 55.5 to 32.5 on HarmBench and from 81 to 25 on JailbreakBench, while GPQA dropped from 32.4 to 27.5 and BBH from 51.5 to 47.8. Only the in-distribution attack was tested.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: LLaDA-8B-Instruct after refusal-aware denoising alignment on 10k DIJA-style prompts, evaluated on DIJA
source_check.reason: Appendix A and Table 4 report residual DIJA ASR-e of 32.5% versus 55.5% on HarmBench and 25.0% versus 81.0% on JailbreakBench. Table 5 reports GPQA 32.4→27.5 and BBH 51.5→47.8. These measured residual failures qualify effectiveness; unseen attack generalization remains untested.
